source.title: Mitigating Adaptive Attacks against Reasoning Models with Activation Consistency Training
source.authors: Avidan Shah; Jannik Brinkmann; Rico Angell

record.tranche_reason: Tests whether a learned linear activation direction causally controls refusal in reasoning models, but derives the direction from ACT-versus-base activations rather than from harmful-minus-harmless means.
record.gate_note: The direction-steering results in Table 9 bear on V1 and V8. The paper's prompt-injection and jailbreak defense results, and its compliant-CoT-prefill results, do not test a refusal direction; the latter is recorded under fits_no_version. Direction extraction details without an outcome are not separate rows.
record.test_reason: Section 6.2 and Appendix A.9 steer reasoning models with one linear direction and report refusal rates under addition and subtraction. This bears on V8, and on V1's addition and removal claims, by a different method. The direction is not harmful-minus-harmless. It is the mean activation difference between an ACT-fine-tuned model and its base model at the chat-template suffix, so it is a training-induced direction rather than the model's native refusal direction. Removal is subtraction of α·d at later layers, not projection at all layers and positions. All B rows remove a fine-tuned defense, not native refusal.
record.authors_conclusion: Broadly right. The authors say ACT training produces a roughly linear refusal direction at the assistant-turn boundary. Adding it to the base model induces refusal on jailbreaks and subtracting it from the ACT model restores compliance, cleanly on both Qwen3 models. Phi-4, Gemma-4 and GPT-OSS replicate only partially, which they attribute to per-model hyperparameter sensitivity. They frame the direction as created by ACT and comparable to Arditi et al.'s; they do not claim it is the native harmful-minus-harmless direction.
record.recipe_differences: The direction is extracted as the ACT-model minus undefended-base activation difference at shared suffix positions across jailbreak training examples, rather than harmful-minus-harmless mean activations. The study steers at later layers and does not project the direction out of every layer and position.
record.method_sensitivity: Outcome depends on model and steering strength α; the paper also notes sensitivity to extraction position, extraction-layer set, application-layer set, and α schedule.

fits_no_version.finding: ACT-defended models refuse at least 98% of jailbreaks after a compliant base-model CoT is prefilled. On Qwen3-8B they still refuse after partial-CoT prefill (95%) and after a response-prefix prefill (82/82).
fits_no_version.proposed_claim: Activation-level consistency training places the refusal decision upstream of the chain of thought, so it is robust to compliant reasoning traces.

record.problems: The tested direction is not the harmful-minus-harmless direction in V1, and steering is applied at later layers rather than as all-layer/all-position ablation. General capability preservation under steering is not evaluated. The paper reports incomplete or degenerate steering results for several models; Phi-4 results are affected by empty outputs, and refusal is classified by prefix matching with manual inspection of a sample.
record.rows_left_out: No additional direction-steering conditions were omitted. Prompt-injection and jailbreak defense results, and the CoT-prefill result, are not rows for V1 or V8 because they do not test the direction itself; the CoT-prefill finding is recorded under fits_no_version.

untested.parts: Harmful-minus-harmless difference-in-means direction; directional ablation (projection) at all layers and positions; preservation of general abilities under the intervention; native refusal, since the direction is the ACT fine-tuning shift.
Whether the model's own harmful-minus-harmless direction mediates refusal in reasoning models; ablation rather than subtraction; capability preservation under steering.

missing.what: Unsteered refusal baselines (base and ACT) for Qwen3-1.7B, Phi-4-reasoning and GPT-OSS-20B under the prefix-match judge. Only Qwen3-8B (1%/96%) and Gemma base (7%) are stated.
missing.locator: Appendix A.9, Table 9 and per-model interpretation

missing.what: Partial-CoT and response-prefix prefill results on Qwen3-8B (95% refusal after about 342 tokens; 82/82 refusals)

record.verdict_notes: The key caveat for any researcher: d_ACT is the mean activation shift produced by the authors' own refusal-inducing fine-tune, averaged over jailbreak training examples. The B-condition results therefore show the fine-tuning delta can be undone linearly, not that native refusal is removable. Gemma-4-E4B-it is called a reasoning model by the paper. The refusal judge is prefix matching plus manual spot checks. Phi-4 has empty-output caveats. MMLU is reported only for trained checkpoints, not under steering.

versions.untested_parts: The tested direction is the mean ACT-minus-base activation difference over jailbreak training examples at shared-suffix positions, not a harmful-minus-harmless difference-in-means direction. The paper steers at later layers rather than projecting the direction out of every layer and position. General capability preservation under direction removal is not measured; benign false-refusal rates are reported.
No weight edit or released-model abliteration is tested.
The adaptive attackers are not tested as suppressing the refusal direction, and training against direction ablation is not evaluated.
The paper does not compare single-direction accounts with affine, cone, or multiple-direction accounts.
No separate harmfulness-judgment representation is measured.
No transfer across languages, base/instruct variants, or other specified model variants is tested.
The paper does not vary refusal-training methods or timing to test when a removable direction arises.
The reasoning-model experiment uses an ACT-induced direction, not the original harmful-minus-harmless direction, and does not test all-layer/all-position ablation or broad capability preservation.
